items.rationale: The order is written into the program that runs the calls, so a new step is added there. Options a and b hand the choice of the next step to the model, and d hides a fixed step inside another step, which still leaves the program's order as the thing to change.

When the order is known and never varies, letting the model choose it adds a model call per decision for no gain. Options b and c are risks that a fixed order also avoids, but they are not about cost, and a is not generally true.

The next lookup depends on findings that vary in too many ways to branch on in advance, which is where model-chosen steps pay off. Free text, several tools and written output are all handled inside fixed workflows too, so b, c and d wrongly equate using a model or tools with being an agent.

items.answer: With a fixed order, each step runs the same way every time with known inputs and outputs, so you can check steps in turn and find the one that went wrong; in a loop the path differs per run.
accepted: The steps always run in the same known order, so you can find which step went wrong
Because the path is the same every run, you can locate the faulty step
A fixed order is predictable, so each step can be checked on its own
In a loop the path changes every run, so it is harder to trace which step failed
items.rationale: A fixed order is predictable and each step can be tested and inspected separately, whereas a model-directed run takes a different path each time. An answer that only mentions cost does not address debugging.

Only the multi-page questions need a variable number of fetches, so give the model control of extra fetches there and keep the rest fixed. Fetching five pages always adds cost to every question, a better label does not give the fixed path an extra fetch, and a loop for every question adds agent cost to the easy ones.

Code owns the outer order and the cap, but the model owns how many searches happen, so control is shared. The worst case is 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 calls, which is a ceiling on calls, but a request that finishes after one search makes fewer.
